bio.en: Lauren Ipsen is a veteran people and talent leader who has built and scaled hiring and talent functions at high-growth technology companies.
bio.zh: 劳伦·伊普森（Lauren Ipsen）是一位资深的人力资源与人才领导者，曾在多家高增长的科技公司搭建并扩展招聘与人才体系。

summary.en: Lauren argues you should always keep a pulse on the talent market, whether or not you're hiring, so you know what "good" looks like. She encourages founders to build relationships with exceptional people long before a specific need arises. The episode is a playbook for proactive, high-quality hiring and staying close to great talent.
summary.zh: 劳伦认为，无论是否在招聘，都应持续关注人才市场动态，这样才能知道什么是"好"的标准。她鼓励创始人在具体需求出现之前，就与杰出人才建立关系。本期是一份关于主动、高质量招聘，并贴近优秀人才的手册。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Regardless of whether or not you're hiring, you should always be keeping a pulse on the market. That is the most important thing. And I think that should be the case for both candidates and folks that are hiring. Like, you never want to put yourself in a position where you have no idea what good looks like, whether that's from a company standpoint or from a candidate standpoint. So, both parties should always be having a good understanding of which companies are thriving, which individuals are building great things and are well known commodities in their organizations and get great references.
turns.zh: 无论你是否在招人，你都应该一直对市场保持脉搏。那是最重要的事。我觉得对候选人和招人方都该如此。就像，你永远不想让自己处于不知道"好"长什么样的境地，无论是从公司角度还是候选人角度。所以，双方都应一直清楚哪些公司在蓬勃发展、哪些个人在打造好东西、是他们组织里众所周知的"硬通货"、并拿到很好的推荐。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Oftentimes, I encourage founders to simply chat with what good looks like and get a really good sense of what benchmark candidate profiles could be, and who knows where that person will be in a year or what have you, but staying really, really close to really great people and using them from an advising capacity or getting them ingrained in some type of involvement in the product prior to actually having that specific need, I think, is really important.
turns.zh: 很多时候，我鼓励创始人只是去聊聊"好"长什么样、对标杆候选人的画像有个很好的感觉，谁知道那人一年后会在哪或怎样，但和真正优秀的人保持非常、非常近，在真有那具体需要前，从顾问身份用他们、或让他们在产品里有某种参与，我觉得非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Welcome to Lenny's Podcast. I'm Lenny and my goal here is to help you get better at the craft of building and growing products. Today my guest is Lauren Ipsen.
turns.zh: 欢迎来到 Lenny 的播客。我是 Lenny，我的目标是帮你把建和增长产品的手艺做得更好。今天的嘉宾是 Lauren Ipsen。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of the most important skills for founders and senior product leaders to develop is the ability to hire great people. You won't be able to build the best company or the best product if you can't hire the best people. And Lauren is one of the most experienced and successful people in the world when it comes to hiring product leaders. She's placed over 80 senior product leaders across tech companies and has worked with some of the biggest companies out there. When I asked a bunch of really smart product leaders who their favorite product recruiter was, Lauren's name came up a ton.
turns.zh: 创始人和资深产品领导者要培养的最重要技能之一，是招到优秀人的能力。如果你招不到最好的人，你就建不出最好的公司或最好的产品。而在招产品领导者这件事上，Lauren 是世界上最有经验、最成功的人之一。她为科技公司安置了 80 多位资深产品领导者，并和外面一些最大的公司合作过。当我问一堆超聪明的产品领导者他们最喜欢的产品招聘官是谁，Lauren 的名字被提了超多次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In our conversation, we get super tactical about what founders need to do to find the best product talent, what product managers should be doing during their career to give themselves the most opportunity, and we also touch on what recruiters themselves often get wrong when trying to attract great talent. This episode is rich with actionable advice for basically everyone, and I am really excited to bring it to you. With that, I bring you Lauren Ipsen.
turns.zh: 在我们的对话里，我们非常落地地聊创始人需要做什么去找最好的产品人才、产品管理者在职业生涯中该做什么给自己最多机会，我们也触及招聘官自己在吸引优秀人才时常犯的错。这期对基本所有人富含可行动的建议，我非常兴奋带给你。话不多说，有请 Lauren Ipsen。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Who has an opinion on internal tools? Internal tools are something you probably don't think about until you have to, or it probably didn't even occur to you to think about them, but if you work at a big company, you probably have a bunch of one-off custom apps or dashboards that are laser focused on just one job to be done for one specific team or just one role, and they're always such a huge pain to build and maintain. And that's why I'm such a big fan of Retool, and why I think Retool is so popular. Retool allows teams as small as just one person to build a suite of custom internal apps in a fraction of the time that you think it takes. The productivity gains of custom apps is now within reach, not just for large enterprises, but for small teams as well. And as you scale your company, Retool scales with you.
turns.zh: 谁对内部工具有意见？内部工具是你大概不会想到、直到你不得不用，或大概根本没想过要去想它们，但如果你在大公司工作，你大概有一堆一次性的定制 App 或仪表盘，激光般聚焦就一个团队或就一个角色的一件待办工作，而它们总是建和维护起来巨大的痛。那正是我这么挺 Retool、以及我觉得 Retool 这么受欢迎的原因。Retool 让小到一人的团队，在你以为要花的时间的一小部分里，建一套定制内部 App。定制 App 的生产力收益现在触手可及，不只大企业，小团队也是。而随你公司规模化，Retool 随你扩展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Snowflake saves about 26 hours a week of manual spreadsheet work with custom internal apps built on Retool. Amazon uses Retool to handle GDPR requests. Thousands of teams at companies like Coinbase, DoorDash, and NBC collaborate around custom-built Retool apps to operate with greater efficiency.
turns.zh: Snowflake 用建在 Retool 上的定制内部 App，每周省约 26 小时手动表格工作。Amazon 用 Retool 处理 GDPR 请求。Coinbase、DoorDash、NBC 等公司上千个团队围绕定制的 Retool App 协作，以更高效率运作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe you've thought about using Retool before but just haven't, and I'm here to tell you that now teams of up to five can build unlimited Retool apps for free. Get started today at retool.com/lenny.
turns.zh: 也许你之前想过用 Retool 但没用，我在这告诉你，现在最多 5 人的团队能免费建无限 Retool App。今天在 retool.com/lenny 开始。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today's episode is brought to you by Miro. Creating a product, especially one that your users can't live without, is damn hard, but it's made easier by working closely with your colleagues to capture ideas, get feedback, and being able to iterate quickly. That's where Miro comes in. Miro is an online visual whiteboard that's designed specifically for teams like yours.
turns.zh: 本期由 Miro 赞助。创造一个产品，尤其一个用户离不开的，真难，但和同事紧密合作、抓想法、拿反馈、能快速迭代，让它变容易。那就是 Miro 来的地方。Miro 是个在线视觉白板，专为像你这样的团队设计。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I actually used Miro to come up with a plan for this very ad. With Miro, you can build out your product strategy by brainstorming sticky notes, comments, live reactions, voting tools, even a timer to keep your team on track. You can also bring your whole distributed team together around wire frames where anyone can draw their own ideas with the pen tool or put their own images or mock-ups right into the Miro board. And with one of Miro's ready made templates, you can go from discovering research to product roadmaps to customer journey flows to final mocks.
turns.zh: 我其实用 Miro 想出了这则广告的计划。用 Miro，你能通过头脑风暴便利贴、评论、实时反应、投票工具、甚至一个计时器让团队不跑题，来建你的产品策略。你也能把整个分布式团队聚到线框图周围，任何人都能用画笔工具画自己的想法、或把自己的图或模型直接放进 Miro 板。用 Miro 一个现成模板，你能从发现研究到产品路线图、到客户旅程流、到最终模型。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Want to see how I use Miro? Head on over to my Miro board at miro.com/lenny to see my most popular podcast episodes, my favorite Miro templates. You can also leave feedback on this podcast episode and more. That's M-I-R-O.com/lenny.
turns.zh: 想看我怎么用 Miro？去我的 Miro 板 miro.com/lenny 看我最受欢迎的播客集、我最爱的 Miro 模板。你也能对这期播客留反馈等等。那是 M-I-R-O.com/lenny。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Lauren, thank you for being here. Welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: Lauren，谢谢你来。欢迎上播客。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Thanks so much. It's great to be here.
turns.zh: 太感谢了。很高兴来这。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've been meeting to do an episode on product hiring and recruiting product people for a while, and when I asked a bunch of smart friends who should I have on to talk about this stuff, your name came up a bunch, and so I'm really happy that we're finally doing this.
turns.zh: 我想做一期产品招聘、招产品人的节目有一阵了，而当我问一堆聪明朋友该请谁聊这些，你的名字被提了一堆，所以我真高兴我们终于做了。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Me too. Absolutely. I'm grateful that you asked.
turns.zh: 我也是。绝对。我感激你邀请。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, to help listeners get a sense of just your background and kind of the journey you've been on to get to where you are now, can you just spend maybe just a minute kind of talking through the wonderful things you've done in your career and what you're doing now?
turns.zh: 所以，帮听众了解下你的背景、你走到今天的旅程，你能花大概一分钟讲下你职业生涯里做的事、和现在在做什么吗？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. So I started my career in broadcast. I originally thought that I wanted to be on the news and quickly realized I didn't necessarily want to be the face of sadness. There's a ton of that happening in the world.
turns.zh: 对，绝对。我职业生涯起步于广播。我原以为我想上新闻，很快意识到我不一定想当悲伤的面孔。世界上有太多那种事。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So, made a pivot pretty early on and thought, where could I use the communication skills that I've been working so hard on and do something that's impactful in a big way, but maybe just with a little bit of a different angle? And stumbled across executive search.
turns.zh: 所以，挺早做了转向，想，我能把一直苦练的沟通技巧用哪、做点有大事影响、但也许就角度略不同？然后撞见高管寻聘（executive search）。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Exec search is not really something that people major in college by any means or think they're going to end up doing. So it was something I found fascinating. I had applied to all of these different companies like Twitter and Snap and Pinterest, hadn't heard back from any of them, was a name in the resumes, and thought, well, how cool would it be if I could work with all of them and have an opportunity to play a part from a different lens?
turns.zh: 高管寻聘绝不是人大学主修、或以为自己最终会做的。所以我觉得它迷人。我投了所有那些不同公司像 Twitter、Snap、Pinterest，没一个回音，是简历堆里一个名字，然后想，嗯，如果我能和所有他们合作、有机会从另一个镜头扮演角色，多酷？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So, got into exec search, was really focused early on on consumer mobile build outs. Was doing a lot of work with Twitter and Reddit and TaskRabbit and Nextdoor, Postmates, you name it, and that was probably 85% of the work I was doing. And then as, on the agency side, 15% was obscure, autonomous helicopters selling into the Department of Defense and then retail and robotics, and it was all very fascinating, but for me, who has wicked bad ADD, it was amazing to be able to be so stimulated by so many different industries and feel like I couldn't really master this.
turns.zh: 所以，进了高管寻聘，早期非常聚焦消费移动端的搭建。和 Twitter、Reddit、TaskRabbit、Nextdoor、Postmates 做很多工作，你叫得出，那大概是我 85% 的工作。然后代理侧，15% 是冷门的、卖去国防部的自主直升机、然后零售和机器人，都迷人，但对我这 ADD 超严重的人，能这么多不同行业刺激、感觉真掌握不了，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So, long story short, had an awesome career at Daversa Partners, which is a boutique executive search firm, and thought I was going to be there potentially forever. Was tapped by a awesome individual, Abe Shafi, who was founding a company. I had been doing a lot of work for them. They were a client of mine at the time. Placed a couple great hires and they said, "We're either going to kick off a head of talent search with you or you can come over and join us." So I was the first recruiting hire over there, built out the talent function in its entirety.
turns.zh: 长话短说，在 Daversa Partners——一家精品高管寻聘公司——有超棒职业生涯，以为可能永远在那。被一个超棒的人 Abe Shafi 挖，他在创公司。我之前为他们做很多工作。他们当时是我客户。安置了几个好 hire，他们说"我们要么和你启动一个人才负责人寻聘，要么你过来加入我们。"所以我是那的第一个招聘 hire，把人才职能整个建起来。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: I definitely think there was a part of me that I loved the operating experience, learned a ton, worked side by side some amazing people, but was really missing working with founders, and lots of them, and keeping a pulse on the market. So General Catalyst tapped me most recently, and been working here for the past couple months, and it's been great thus far, and I'm specializing in our consumer and crypto investments.
turns.zh: 我绝对觉得我有一部分爱那运营经验，学了一吨、和超棒的人并肩，但真想念和创始人、很多创始人合作、保持市场脉搏。所以 General Catalyst 最近挖我，过去几个月在这工作，至今很棒，我专攻消费和 crypto 投资。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. The fact that you're at GC now makes me think about another recruiter that I know who's awesome, Austin Brizendine, and it's interesting that a lot of the best recruiters seem to be heading to VC funds, and I'm curious why that is happening. Is it like a comp thing? Is it other things that are pulling everyone away into funds?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你现在在 GC 这事实让我想到另一个我认识的超棒招聘官 Austin Brizendine，而有趣的是很多最好的招聘官似乎都去 VC 基金了，我好奇为什么发生。是薪酬事吗？还是别的把大家拉去基金？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: It's a great question. It's definitely not a comp thing. I'll say that. I think it could be a stability of life thing. Search is incredibly volatile, and you have to hustle so hard, and as soon as you have three wins, you've got four more things to execute on. And so, there's aspects of it that can be tough, especially in a market like right now where you really do have to chase business and you can't be selective about what you take on, so you could be pitching things that maybe you don't necessarily believe in in its entirety or what have you. So, I think that's one component.
turns.zh: 好问题。绝对不是薪酬事。我得说。我觉得也许是生活稳定性事。寻聘极其波动，你得超努力 hustle，而一旦你有三个赢，你又有四个要执行的事。所以有方面难，尤其在现在这种市场，你真得追生意、不能挑你接的，所以你可能在 pitch 你不一定完全相信的东西。所以，我觉得那是一部分。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: In house is obviously difficult right now as well for talent leaders. It's really scary to take a bet on one single company right now and know what it's going to look like six months from now. And so I think those things combined might be the reason for an influx in folks leaning more towards venture, and I think it's just timeliness.
turns.zh: 内部（in-house）对人才领导者现在显然也难。现在押注一家单一公司、知道六个月后它什么样，真吓人。所以我觉得那些事结合也许是大家更多倾向风投的原因，我觉得只是时机。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. That makes sense. The downside is it's hard for people to find awesome recruiters because once you're in a fund, you're just going to help those startups. And so we're going to talk later about just how do people find awesome recruiters, what do you look for? But there's roughly three things I want to spend our time chatting through today. One is for founders and hiring managers, just how to find the best talent and what they could do to be successful finding the best talent. Two is for product leaders and PMs, how to give themselves the most opportunity from the flip side. And then third is just for recruiters, what do they often do wrong? How do they miss out on the best product talent? Does that sound good?
turns.zh: 懂了。说得通。坏处是人们难找到超棒招聘官，因为一旦你在基金，你就只帮那些初创。而我们稍后会聊人们怎么找超棒招聘官、你看什么？但今天大致有三件事我想花时间聊。一是给创始人和 hiring manager，怎么找最好人才、他们能做什么成功找到最好人才。二是给产品领导者和 PM，怎么从另一面给自己最多机会。三是给招聘官，他们常做错什么？他们怎么错过最好的产品人才？听起来好吗？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah, that sounds great.
turns.zh: 对，听起来很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. So on the hiring front, just diving in, say you are a founder, you're someone really early at a company, and maybe you've got a couple PMs and you're starting to think about we need to hire a really senior product leader or first senior product leader.
turns.zh: 好，酷。所以在招聘前线，直接深入，假设你是个创始人、公司非常早期的人，也许你已有几个 PM、开始想我们需要招一个真正资深的产品领导者、或第一个资深产品领导者。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you find is often the biggest mistake that founders make when they're trying to hire their first senior product leader?
turns.zh: 你发现创始人招第一个资深产品领导者时常犯的最大错误是什么？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: I think especially for founders that haven't hired for this caliber of talent in the past, it's really easy to be distracted by shiny objects and look at huge names. You want to find the CPOs of Google and YouTube or what have you because that seems like it would be such an incredible opportunity for brand recognition. And to an extent, it is. But the fact of the matter is, oftentimes those individuals are pretty far from the work and have a great team of executors that they've put into place that are actually the ones that are in the weeds.
turns.zh: 我觉得尤其对过去没招过这种级别人才的创始人，很容易被闪亮的东西分心、看大名字。你想找 Google 和 YouTube 的 CPO 或之类，因为那似乎是个品牌认知的惊人机会。在某种程度上，它是。但事实是，往往那些人离工作相当远，他们放了一支超棒的 executor 团队，实际在 weeds 里的是那些人。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: And so I think that's the biggest mistake I see people make, especially on the hiring front where they have limited resources, and maybe they're an early stage company and trying so hard to bring in big names is not always the best way to go about it because the fact of the matter is they need to go then hire a team. So, I think looking for someone that's a little closer to the work, maybe someone that can step up into that type of role and do so in a way where some days they might actually be operating like a PM and then other days they might be able to build from a leadership perspective, that's more of the DNA that people should be targeting.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得那是我看到人们犯的最大错误，尤其在招聘前线、他们资源有限，也许他们是早期公司，拼命想带进大名字不总是最好的办法，因为事实是他们然后得去招一支团队。所以，我觉得找离工作更近的人、也许能 stepped up 进那种角色、并以有些天他们其实像 PM 运作、其他天能从领导视角建的方式做的人，那是人们更该瞄准的 DNA。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you think the source of the issue with that going wrong, that they no longer can do that work as well because they've been shielded away from the tactical day to day? Or is it that they're not as hungry as they used to be and they're just like, "I already, I'm a YouTube 10 year super success, I don't need to prove myself anymore," and they're just not as hungry, or something else?
turns.zh: 你觉得那出错的根源，是他们不再能做好那工作因为被战术日常屏蔽了？还是他们没以前那么饥渴、就"我已经，我是 YouTube 十年超级成功，我不用再证明自己了"、就不那么饥渴，还是别的？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: I mean, I'm not going to sit here and say that all senior leaders aren't hungry. I think that there's some folks that really lean into the work in a different way and miss that, and often go to startups because they crave building.
turns.zh: 我是说，我不会坐这说所有资深领导者都不饥渴。我觉得有些人以不同方式真 lean into 工作、想念那，常去初创因为他们渴望建。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So it's not necessarily that, but I do tend to lean towards folks that have a chip on their shoulder or have something to prove and want to build a name for themselves. All of that to say, there's a reason that a lot of those people got to where they are, and some of the best talent are some of the senior folks, but just maybe not necessarily the best talent for where this company is today. Right? It could be great for 10 years down the road, but the past five years of that individual's career could have been far more focused on camaraderie, team building, operational components, performance reviews, and then aspects of product vision, which just might not be the innovative AB testing type of profile that you typically look for in these pre-IPO companies.
turns.zh: 所以不一定那样，但我确实倾向有 chip on their shoulder（不服气）、或有要证明的东西、想为自己建名声的人。所有那些说，那些人到达那位置有原因，有些最好人才是些资深的人，但也许不一定是对这公司今天最好的。对吧？它可能对十年后很棒，但那人职业生涯过去五年可能更聚焦同志情谊、团队建设、运营组件、绩效评估，然后产品愿景的方面，那可能就不是你典型在这些 pre-IPO 公司找的创新 AB 测试型画像。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. I imagine there are stories that you can share about people you've placed like that, that have not worked out. If you can share one, that'd be awesome. But maybe a side question is the general advice, just don't assume someone that's been successful at a big company with a fancy background is going to be great. Sometimes they work out, but not always, is that kind of the takeaway?
turns.zh: 懂了。我想象你能分享你安置的、像那样没成的事。如果你能分享一个，那会超棒。但也许个旁支问题是一般建议，别假设在大公司有 fancy 背景成功的人会超棒。有时他们成，但不总是，那是大概的收获？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah. I would say the general advice is who is going to be best for this specific role at this specific time, not necessarily who is the best talent in the world or in the market. Those are two very, very different questions to ask. And I think early on in my recruiting career, I was often just trying to recruit these whales of executives to try and prove myself and say, "Oh, I got this person to entertain this opportunity, how sick is that?" But naturally, that's not necessarily the person that actually can move the needle. And so you need to think very specifically. Just because this is the best talent, that doesn't necessarily mean they are the best talent for this role today.
turns.zh: 对。我会说一般建议是，谁是对这特定角色、在这特定时刻最好的，不一定谁是世界上或市场里最好的人才。那是两个非常、非常不同的问题。我觉得在我招聘生涯早期，我常只是试图招这些高管鲸鱼来证明自己、说"哦，我让这人考虑这机会，多 sick。"但自然，那不一定是真能移动指针的人。所以你得想得非常具体。就因为这最好的人才，不一定意味着他们是对这角色今天最好的人才。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So to double down on that, say you are hiring and you know you're going to start hiring a senior product leader, what is it that you suggest founders nail down and iron out when they're kicking off the hiring process, either on their own or with a recruiter? Like, in the job description, what else do they have to get right to find the right person?
turns.zh: 为强调那个，假设你招、你知道你要开始招一个资深产品领导者，你建议创始人在启动招聘流程时——自己或和招聘官——钉死和搞清什么？像，在职位描述里，他们还得搞对什么以找到对的人？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: It's a number of things, like product leaders can come in a lot of different flavors, and so I think it's trying to determine where this person should major and minor, where they should spike. Is this someone that's going to really lean into the design efforts? Is it someone that actually kind of needs to just operate like a very senior PM and continue to build out a team? Is this someone that really should be focused on product vision for the long haul? And then thinking more holistically about how to build the rest of the team.
turns.zh: 是好多事，像产品领导者能以很多不同 flavor 来，所以我觉得是试图决定这人该 major 和 minor 在哪、该在哪拔尖。这是真 lean into 设计努力的人？这是其实有点只需像非常资深 PM 运作、继续建团队的人？这是真该长期聚焦产品愿景的人？然后更整体想怎么建团队其余。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: There's so many different ways in which you can hire for a product leader. So I think it's trying to work a little bit backwards and think about, what is the actual outcome that we are trying to solve for with this hire? Or are we just hiring a head of product because we feel like we need to hire a head of product? That's so often what I see is the board's telling me we need to hire a head of product and I don't necessarily think that we do, or I'm not exactly sure what we need in this role. And so whenever you're starting a search in that regard, it's kind of doomed from inception, so you need to get incredibly granular on the front end around, what is this person going to be coming in to do? What's their mandate? And if we think about someone that's just absolutely hitting it out of the park and crushing it, what does that look like? So I think just trying to be really specific on the front end.
turns.zh: 有太多不同方式招产品领导者。所以我觉得是试图稍微往后推、想，我们试图用这 hire 解决的实际结果是什么？还是我们只是因为觉得需要招个产品负责人而招？那常是我看到的——董事会告诉我我们需要招产品负责人、而我不一定觉得我们需要，或我不确切知道这角色要什么。所以每当你那样启动寻聘，它从一开始就有点注定失败，所以你需在前端极其细化——这人要进来做什么？他们的使命是什么？如果我们想有人绝对大杀四方、碾压，那长什么样？所以我觉得前端尽量具体。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that last piece, just what does success really look like for this person? On the first piece, that's exactly the same advice I give founders when they're looking for a PM is like, what do you concretely need them to do day to day? Not like, "We need someone to help us with product." And that often helps illuminate, okay, I see. We need someone to help us ship more consistently. We need someone to help us hire engineers. Yeah, just make a list. What are they going to do in the first month or two or three?
turns.zh: 我爱最后那点，就是这人的成功到底长什么样？在第一点，那正是我给创始人找 PM 的同样建议——像，你具体需要他们日复一日做什么？不是"我们需要人帮我们做产品。"那常帮阐明，哦我懂，我们需要人帮我们更稳定地交付。我们需要人帮我们招工程师。对，就列个单。他们头一两个月或三月要做什么？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, absolutely. I think those are the most important things. Like the 90 day plan is something that's overused but so necessary, and that's just the tip of the iceberg. So that component and then, okay, a year from now, what should this person be doing? Two years from now? Do we want them to grow up into a CPO role? Do we think about that in a different way? How are we thinking about the product direction today, 12 months from now, 18 months from now, through IPO? I think it's really difficult to think about things that way, and so often you're thinking about the task in front of you and just trying to iterate quickly, but that is the type of thought process that needs to be happening from the CEOs and founders.
turns.zh: 对，对，绝对。我觉得那些是最重要的事。像 90 天计划被用滥但如此必要，而那只是冰山一角。所以那组件、然后，好，一年后，这人该做什么？两年后？我们想要他们长成 CPO 角色吗？我们以不同方式想吗？我们今天怎么想产品方向、12 个月后、18 个月后、到 IPO？我觉得那样想真难，所以常你想眼前任务、只想快速迭代，但那正是 CEO 和创始人需要的思考过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there archetypes of PMs, if you just bucket like here's the three maybe most common types of product leaders that founders hire, because there's an infinite list of skills and things they could do, but just to make it even simpler, like here's probably one of these three you're looking for. Do you have something like that in your head?
turns.zh: 有没有 PM 的原型，如果你就分桶像这大概最常见的三种产品领导者创始人招的，因为有无限技能和他们能做的事列表，但就简化，像这大概三种之一你在找。你脑里有那样的吗？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah, there's platform product leaders or folks that are kind of more indexed on the infrastructure components. There's folks that are typically focused on core product, or consumer product if it's on the consumer side of things. And then you'll have folks that are really indexed and that can include UX individuals, design folks. And then there's also typically specialists, so individuals that are really hyper-focused on growth or monetization or what have you. Those are the three buckets that I would say I see most often.
turns.zh: 对，有平台产品领导者、或有点更 indexed on 基础设施组件的人。有通常聚焦核心产品、或如果是消费侧就消费者产品的人。然后你有真 indexed、那能包括 UX 个人、设计的人。然后通常也有专家，所以超聚焦增长或变现或之类的人。那些是我会说最常看到的三个桶。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you feel like founders sometimes pick one of the wrong buckets and that's a common mistake, or is it generally it's the wrong bucket but then maybe it's not the right spikes of skills within that bucket?
turns.zh: 你觉得创始人有时挑了错桶、那是常见错误，还是通常是错桶、但也许是那桶里没对的技能拔尖？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Well, it's kind of twofold. I think sometimes people just bring in a head of product to do everything, so that's probably not the best way to go about things. I think that ends up being a unicorn, which you hear often in the search world, and it becomes really difficult to hone in on what good looks like.
turns.zh: 嗯，是两方面。我觉得有时人就把产品负责人带进来做一切，所以那也许不是最好的办法。我觉得那最终成独角兽（unicorn），你在寻聘世界常听到，而它变得真难聚焦"好"长什么样。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: And so I think again, it just comes back to having a clear org chart on the front end and determining, are we hiring someone specifically to build out our walled garden ads approach, or are we hiring someone to run product marketing, or are we hiring someone to help from a product perspective to build a better core user experience? Those are all very, very, very different roles, and if you bring in one person to try and do it all, the facts of the matter is, they're going to have to bring in some key lieutenants to help them, so is that something you want to do or are you more focused on bringing in someone imminently to help on the ad side of things, and then we can find that head of product to help them out down the road?
turns.zh: 所以我觉得 again，它回到前端有清晰的组织图、决定，我们是招人专门建我们的围墙花园广告方式，还是招人跑产品营销，还是招人从产品视角帮建更好的核心用户体验？那些都是非常、非常、非常不同的角色，而如果你带一个人试做全部，事实是，他们得带些关键副手帮他们，所以那是你想做的吗、还是你更聚焦带个马上能帮广告侧的人、然后我们路上再找那产品负责人帮他们？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: That's kind of the way in which I would architect it and think about it, is what's most imminent, and what do you actually need to hire for today, as opposed to just hiring for the sake of hiring and bringing in that leader.
turns.zh: 那是大概我 architect 它、想它的方式——什么最迫在眉睫、你今天实际需要招什么，而非为招而招、带那领导者进来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And part of the discussion there is maybe they grow up into this head of product long term, maybe not. Maybe we just need someone to ship the ads platform, right?
turns.zh: 那讨论的一部分也许是他们对产品负责人长期长成，也许不。也许我们就需要人发广告平台，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: That's exactly right. Yeah.
turns.zh: 正是。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned this title of head of product. There's also VP of product, CPO. There's all these titles and I feel like people sometimes use them interchangeably, don't know which one to use when they're putting out a job description. Do you have any kind of heuristic rule of thumb of just, here's how to think about when to use each of these titles? Or is it not even a big deal for, say, a founder, hiring the first senior product leader?
turns.zh: 你提了产品负责人这头衔。还有产品 VP、CPO。有所有这些头衔，我觉得人有时互换用、不知道放职位描述时用哪个。你对就怎么想何时用每个头衔，有启发式的经验法则吗？或对比如创始人招第一个资深产品领导者，那甚至不是大事？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: It's a great question and it definitely leads to confusion across the board because I'll have candidates come to me and they'll say, "I'm only looking for a CPO role," when I'm working with a startup where, maybe on the venture side of things, we've actually advised that startup to not hire C-level executives at this point. And so that naturally could eliminate a candidate that could be amazing for the role.
turns.zh: 好问题，它绝对导致全盘困惑，因为会有候选人来找我说"我只找 CPO 角色"，而我合作的初创，也许风投侧我们其实建议那初创现在别招 C 级高管。所以那自然可能淘汰一个对角色超棒的人。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Similarly, people could feel that way if it's a VP of product role, but that in their mind is the most senior product leader within the organization running everything from end to end who they intend to be the CPO down the road but are not in a position where they're ready to hire C-level execs. So, it's tough, and it really depends on the organization and the way in which they're thinking about org charts and leveling.
turns.zh: 同理，如果是产品 VP 角色，他们可能觉得那是组织里最资深产品领导者、端到端跑一切、他们打算路上当 CPO 但还没到能招 C 级高管的位子。所以，它难，真取决于组织和他们想组织图、leveling 的方式。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: A lot of startups at this point are almost allergic to C titles or VP titles or are just more title agnostic than I've seen in the past, so you see a lot more of these head ofs, and that is sector leaders, up until probably C plus or D stage. And then you get to D and E, and you'll see more of the VP, director, CPO type. And I think that is the way that people should be thinking about it is, if I'm joining a company very, very early days and it's called head of engineering, that is intended to be the most senior engineering leader within the organization.
turns.zh: 很多初创在这时点几乎对 C 头衔或 VP 头衔过敏、或比我过去看到的更头衔不可知，所以你看到更多这些 head of、那是 sector leader，直到大概 C+ 或 D 轮。然后你到 D 和 E，你会看到更多 VP、director、CPO 型。我觉得那是人们该想的方式——如果我加入很早的公司、它叫工程负责人（head of engineering），那意图是组织里最资深的工程领导者。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: The fact of the matter though is there's good reason sometimes why they're not throwing out that C title, and could this person be layered down the road? Potentially, because maybe the talent they need right now is different than, just as we had spoken to earlier, is different than the talent that they might need from a massive CPO in two and a half years.
turns.zh: 事实是，有时他们不抛那 C 头衔有好理由，而这人路上能被 layer down 吗？可能，因为也许我们现在需要的人才不同于，就如我们早前聊的，不同于两年半后我们可能从大 CPO 需要的人才。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: And so I think that rubs people the wrong way because they want a bit of a promise that things are going to, if they join at this stage, that they'll be in it for the long haul and be that chief product officer that takes a company through an IPO. But companies are so dynamic and things change so quickly.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得那惹人反感，因为他们想要点承诺——事情会，如果他们在这阶段加入，他们会长期在里面、是带公司过 IPO 的那首席产品官。但公司如此动态、事情变得这么快。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So, I guess a long-winded way of me saying there's different breadth and depth to each role, but I think for the most part, unless it's a very siloed company with multiple different VPs, if you're coming into a company and they say this is the head of product, the VP of product, or the CPO, that all means the same thing dependent on the stage, for the most part.
turns.zh: 所以，我绕远说的意思是每个角色有不同广度和深度，但我觉得大多情况，除非是有一堆不同 VP 的非常筒仓公司，如果你进公司、他们说这是产品负责人、产品 VP、或 CPO，那大多取决于阶段、意思都相同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the other takeaway there, which is awesome, is if you're early stage startup, probably just start with head of product. Keep it simple.
turns.zh: 而另一收获，超棒，是如果你早期初创，可能就从头产品负责人（head of product）开始。保持简单。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Don't over promise. Everyone understands.
turns.zh: 别过度承诺。大家都理解。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah. Because the last thing you want to do is have to demote someone. But once you get to a place of having C-level executives, like that's not going to do any good, but maybe you start as a head of product, and then as the company continues to grow, you lean into the growth side of things more, and so you become that head of growth or an SVP of growth. Like things iterate and change, but you just never know and you can't predict the outcome of a company on the front end, so.
turns.zh: 对。因为最后你想做的是不得不降某人的级。但一旦你到有个 C 级高管的地方，像那不会有什么好，但也许你从头产品负责人开始，然后随公司继续增长，你更多 lean into 增长侧，于是你成那增长负责人或增长 SVP。像事情迭代、变，但你永远不知道、你不能在前端预测公司结果，所以。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of people listening to this probably aren't hiring senior product leaders right now, but plan to and will in the future, and so I wanted to ask, what should founders do when they know they will hire a head of product, say, in the next year, that could set them up for success down the road? What should they be doing ahead of time?
turns.zh: 很多听这的现在大概不在招资深产品领导者，但计划将来会，所以我想问，当创始人知道他们会招产品负责人、比如明年，有什么他们能做的、能为将来成功铺路？他们该提前做什么？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Regardless of whether or not you're hiring, you should always be keeping a pulse on the market. That is the most important thing. And I think that should be the case for both candidates and folks that are hiring. Like, you never want to put yourself in a position where you have no idea what good looks like, whether that's from a company standpoint or from a candidate standpoint. So, both parties should always be having a good understanding of which companies are thriving, which individuals are building great things and are well known commodities in their organizations and get great references.
turns.zh: 无论你是否在招人，你都应该一直对市场保持脉搏。那是最重要的事。我觉得对候选人和招人方都该如此。就像，你永远不想让自己处于不知道"好"长什么样的境地，无论是从公司角度还是候选人角度。所以，双方都应一直清楚哪些公司在蓬勃发展、哪些个人在打造好东西、是他们组织里众所周知的"硬通货"、并拿到很好的推荐。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Oftentimes, I encourage founders to simply chat with what good looks like and get a really good sense of what benchmark candidate profiles could be, and who knows where that person will be in a year or what have you, but staying really, really close to really great people and using them from an advising capacity or getting them ingrained in some type of involvement in the product prior to actually having that specific need, I think, is really important.
turns.zh: 很多时候，我鼓励创始人只是去聊聊"好"长什么样、对标杆候选人的画像有个很好的感觉，谁知道那人一年后会在哪或怎样，但和真正优秀的人保持非常、非常近，在真有那具体需要前，从顾问身份用他们、或让他们在产品里有某种参与，我觉得非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That sounds awesome and it makes sense. How do you, as a founder, do some of that? Do you just ask folks like, "Hey, who are some of the best product leaders you know? I just want to chat with them. I'm not hiring, just want to kind of meet people who are awesome." Is that the behavior you suggest or is there something else you can do?
turns.zh: 那听起来超棒、说得通。你作为创始人，怎么做些那个？你就问人像"嘿，你知道的一些最好的产品领导者是谁？我就想和他们聊聊。我没在招人，就想认识超棒的人。"那是你建议的行为吗，还是有别你能做的？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: That's a great way to go about it. And by simply saying, "No agenda, I'm not trying to hire you tomorrow, I just want to know great people." And to be totally honest, people feel flattered by that, typically. Most of the time if you've been referred to someone and heard nothing but great things about them and you really don't have an agenda other than wanting to pick their brain, people are like, "Huh, well, this is different from the day to day. This is fulfilling," and people want to pour their knowledge, especially into companies that they believe in.
turns.zh: 那是很好的做法。而简单说"没议程，我不是明天要招你，我就想认识超棒的人。"而老实说，人们通常感到受 flattering。大多时候如果你被推荐给某人、只听到关于他们的好话、而你真没议程只想去请教，人们像"哈，嗯，这和日常不同。这满足感"，人们想倒他们的知识，尤其进他们相信的公司。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So, I think more often than not you'll find that, not just products leaders, but executives across the board are actually really inclined to do so and want to help out because it's a little bit different from the day to day monotony of their work life.
turns.zh: 所以，我觉得大多情况你会发现，不只是产品领导者，而是高管整体其实真倾向这么做、想帮忙，因为它有点不同于日常工作的单调。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, the advice is keep track of companies who are killing it, who you might be able to kind of poach from in the future, and keep a list and keep warm contact with folks that are awesome.
turns.zh: 所以，建议是跟踪那些 killing it 的公司、你未来也许能挖的，保持清单、和超棒的人保持温暖联系。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of a founder that ... or basically all founders who are really good at hiring and how far ahead they plant seeds and how they just play the long game with the best people they meet, and they just kind of keep the conversation going until they finally convince them to join a year or two later. Do you find that the same thing?
turns.zh: 它让我想起一个创始人……或基本所有特会招人的创始人、他们多提前播种、和他们遇到的最好的人打长期游戏，他们就保持对话直到最终一两年后说服他们加入。你发现同样的事？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah, 1000000%. Yeah. When I was on the executive recruiting side of things at Daversa, the VP of engineering candidate that we ultimately landed, it was a seven month game of courtship, and let's bring him in to help out from an advising capacity, let's ask him how he would think about structuring this organization, let's talk to him about the best talent that he would recommend that we're spending time with. No question that's invasive, but more so just collaborative and exciting, and you'll find that the founder and that leader will build a different level of rapport and trust by not going through a formal interview process and having it feel transactional. And then with that, magic can happen and you can land incredible people.
turns.zh: 对，一百万%。对。我在 Daversa 高管招聘侧时，我们最终拿下的工程 VP 候选人，是七个月的 courtship 游戏，让我们带他进来顾问身份帮、让我们问他他会怎么想架构这组织、让我们和他聊他会推荐我们花时间的最好的才。毫无疑问那 invasive，但更多是协作和兴奋，而你会发现那创始人和那领导者会通过不走正式面试流程、不让它感觉交易化，建起不同层面的融洽和信任。然后有了那个，魔法会发生、你能拿下惊人人物。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This all sounds like a lot of work and a lot of time. Do you have guidance on how long it should take to find, like for a early stage startup, say series A or B, to find someone awesome, and/or how much time founders should spend a week, just best practice, on hiring for someone like this?
turns.zh: 这一切听起来像很多工作、很多时间。你有指导关于找人多该花多久吗——对早期初创，说 A 或 B 轮，找超棒的人——和/或创始人一周该花多少时间，就最佳实践，招这种人？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: I mean, I think if you're going to search, so if you're looking for this individual, it's really so case to case. There's searches that I've been in that I call three people. I know they're amazing for this. I tell the founder and CEO, "These are the three people you should chat with, hire one of them." And it's that easy.
turns.zh: 我是说，我觉得如果你要 search，所以如果你在找这人，真因案而异。有我参与的 search 我叫三个人。我知道他们对这超棒。我告诉创始人和 CEO"这是你该聊的三个、雇一个。"就那么简单。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: There's others where it's a lot of trying to figure out what the person's actually looking for. If there's some ... they hit it off from an emotional standpoint. There's so many different things that come with it. I would say from a timing perspective, it's not a hard number. It's more of just put yourself in the room with great people. If you have a tremendous amount of respect for someone, continue to harvest that relationship and ask what good looks like. Find excuses to continue to touch base with people that are important in your network. If you remembered that they'd mentioned that they were going to some event and you think that you might want to hire them down the road, in a non-creepy way, show up to that event. These are things that I'm constantly doing, and I think that founders can do a better job of, but just make yourself known and relevant. And then when you reach out and timing is right, it won't feel so obscure or so transactional.
turns.zh: 有别的很多要搞清那人实际在找什么。如果有一些……他们从情感角度 hit it off。有太多不同事随之来。我会说从时间角度，不是硬数字。更多是把自己放进有超棒的人的房间。如果你对某人极大尊重，继续经营那关系、问"好"长什么样。找借口继续和你网络里重要的人碰头。如果你记得他们提过要去某活动、你觉得路上也许想雇他们，以不 creepy 的方式，去那活动。这些是我一直在做的，我觉得创始人能做得更好，但就让自己被知道、相关。然后当你 outreach、时机对，它不会感觉那么 obscure 或交易化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That reminds me of a time at Airbnb where we had these meetups for engineers every month or so where it was a tech talk, and then all the engineers get a target engineer that is coming to the event. Like they get their profile and their picture, and their job is to make sure they have a great time and try to convince them to join someday.
turns.zh: 那让我想起 Airbnb 时我们有这些工程师聚会，大概每月，是个 tech talk，然后所有工程师得到一个目标工程师来活动。像他们拿到他的资料和照片，他们的工作是确保他玩得开心、试图说服他某天加入。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Oh my god. But it's so real. It's similar to college trips where you're trying to get recruited for a sport, and you have to ensure that you're, yeah, just continuing to give people the best experience possible and staying top of mind for people.
turns.zh: 我的天。但它真真实。它类似大学招募旅行，你试图被一项运动招募，你得确保你，对，就继续给人最好的体验、在人心目中保持 top of mind。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. But I can see it being creepy, They have no idea there's this person assigned to them, but it works. It worked great. It was a great tactic.
turns.zh: 对。但我能看出它会 creepy，他们不知道有这个人被分配给他们，但它工作。工作很好。是好战术。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: That's awesome.
turns.zh: 那超棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to a question that I asked, but I feel like you'll have an actual more concrete answer to the specific piece of just, what's your guidance per week how much time you should be spending on hiring broadly, and specifically, heads of product, if that's any different. Do you have any just advice? Because I imagine it's always spend more time than you think. It's going to take a lot of time.
turns.zh: 我想回到我问过的问题，但我感觉你会对具体的那块有更具体的答案——就，你每周指导多少时间该花在招聘上 broadly，具体产品负责人，如果那有任何不同。你有任何建议吗？因为我想象总是花比你想的更多时间。它会花很多时间。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah, it's definitely spend more time than you think. If you are in an actual search, then you should devote all of your time to it. I know that sucks to hear, but you should be really carving out concrete time.
turns.zh: 对，绝对花比你想的更多时间。如果你真在 search，那你该把全部时间献给它。我知道听来糟，但你该真 carving out 具体时间。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: The thing that's tough though is you could spend, I guess what I was trying to say is you could spend one hour on something or you could spend 10 hours on it, but it's more so around, are you doing things to be impactful during that period of time? Are you actually doing things that are going to move the needle? Are you just blindly reaching out to people on LinkedIn? Because that's not going to be the way in which you're going to find the best of the best. Some of the greatest talent, they're not even on LinkedIn.
turns.zh: 难的是你可能花，我猜我想说的是你可能花一小时或花十小时，但更多是，那段时间你在做有影响的事吗？你在做真能移动指针的事吗？你只是在 LinkedIn 盲投人吗？因为那不是你找最好中的最好的方式。有些最棒的人才，他们甚至不在 LinkedIn。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: And so I think it's building a really strong network in advance, and then once you actually get to a place where you need to hire that person, calling all of those amazing people that you've built relationships with and saying, "Now tell me who your favorite person is and who the best person you've ever worked with is, and could you put me on a thread with them?" How are you going to differentiate yourself from the rest of the market? So it's less in my mind like a quantitative number of hours and more of, how are you doing things differently than the rest of the market?
turns.zh: 所以我觉得是提前建强网络，然后一旦你真到需要雇那人的地方，call 所有你建了关系的超棒的人、说"现在告诉我你最喜欢的人是谁、你共事过最好的人是谁、能让我进和他们的 thread 吗？"你怎么从市场其他人对自己差异化？所以在我心里它更少是小时的数量、更多是，你做的事和市场的其他人怎么不同？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to pull on this thread. Okay, so spending one hour versus 10 hours, and your point about how you could spend one hour and get as much done maybe in those 10 hours. What sorts of behaviors and actions should folks take to make use of, say, that one hour in hiring? How do you not waste your time?
turns.zh: 我想拉这线。好，所以花一小时 vs 十小时，和你关于你怎么可能花一小时得到那十小时里那么多的点。人们该采取什么行为和行动来利用，说，那招聘里的一小时？你怎么不浪费时间？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: I mean, I would say I've got probably five of my all time favorite product leaders in the world that I tap whenever I'm kicking off a search. And they know that whenever life brings them to an opportunity where they are going to start looking or want to lean into board opportunities, that I'm going to set them up and shout their name from the rooftop, so oftentimes they're willing to point me in the right direction of great people, make those introductions, what have you, and I'm going to know simply because of how great they are that they would never put me in touch with someone that wasn't equally as qualified.
turns.zh: 我是说，我会说我大概有五个全世界我最爱的产品领导者，我每次启动 search 就 tap。他们知道每当生活带他们到一个机会、他们要开始找或想 lean into 董事会机会，我会 set them up、从屋顶喊他们名字，所以往往他们愿指我去对的人的方向、做那些介绍，之类，而我单纯因为他们超棒就知道他们绝不会让我联系一个同样不 qualified 的人。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So that I think because the quality is there, so I'm not just blindly guessing on quantity, spending a ton of time on LinkedIn, and then having to call unknown entities and ask for back channel references when they also might not even feel comfortable sharing the dirt. You know? So it comes back to rapport and people that you have around you that you know you can trust and tap into and ensuring that you're spending the time in the right areas.
turns.zh: 所以那我觉得因为质量在那，所以我不是盲目猜数量、在 LinkedIn 花大量时间，然后得 call 未知实体、要 back channel 推荐当他们可能甚至不舒服分享 dirt。知道吗？所以它回到融洽、和你周围你知道能信任、能 tap 的人，确保你把时间花在对的区域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Yeah, so tapping your network makes a lot of sense. If you don't have that yet, I guess is it worth spending time on LinkedIn just cold messaging people as a founder, and any tips there for just cold outreach that you think work for a founder doing it versus you who are a professional at it?
turns.zh: 懂了。对，所以 tap 你的网络很有意义。如果你还没有，我猜值得在 LinkedIn 花时间冷消息人吗，作为创始人，和那任何 tips 给创始人做冷 outreach vs 你这专业的？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: I do think it is worth that time. If you see someone that looks amazing, hell yeah, reach out to them, spend time with them, why not? And oftentimes, again, people are excited to see, oh, this CEO and founder wants to pick my brain, doesn't look like they're coming at me to try and recruit me, but rather just to have an open-ended conversation. For sure, and they can sense. You can definitely sense that type of interaction and feel comfortable with it, whereas sometimes the walls immediately go up when someone senses that they're trying to get poached.
turns.zh: 我确实觉得那时间值得。如果你看到某人超棒，见鬼是啊，联系他们、花时间陪他们，为啥不？而往往，again，人们兴奋看到，哦，这 CEO 和创始人想请教我，不像他们冲我来试图招我，而是就开放对话。肯定，他们能 sense。你绝对能 sense 那种互动、对它舒服，而有时当人 sense 他们要被挖，墙立刻立起。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: And so it's I think something that's worth them doing for sure. It's just if you are going to look for a key executive and are on a time crunch, I don't necessarily think the best use of your time is blindly reaching out to executives when you don't necessarily have the expertise in knowing which companies were thriving during that period of time, which organizations were great, and which were a little bit weaker within companies. All of those things are just the inner workings of the recruiting atmosphere and technology, and I think tapping people, if you don't have the network, talk to a great recruiter or just spend some time kind of doing some research on who's great. You can ask investors or board members in your companies as to who you should be targeting. So there's always got to be one or two people that can at least point you to another three or four.
turns.zh: 所以它我觉得肯定值得他们做。只是如果你要找关键高管、时间紧，我不觉得你时间最好用的是盲投高管当你不一定有专业知识知道那时期哪些公司 thriving、哪些组织超棒、哪些在公司里弱。所有那些只是招聘氛围和技术的内部运作，而我觉得 tap 人，如果你没网络，和超棒招聘官聊、或就花时间做点研究谁超棒。你能问你公司的投资人或董事会成员你该目标谁。所以总得有一两个人至少能指你去另外三四个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That reminds me of a tactic Gokul shared on this podcast about one of his best tricks, as you think of, if you're hiring salespeople, instead of looking for who are just the best salespeople, you look for the company that is known for being really good at sales and then you go find people there and try to poach their lieutenant types, not maybe necessarily their head of sales. Do you think that's a good move?
turns.zh: 那让我想起 Gokul 在这播客分享的战术——他最好的技巧之一，你这样想，如果你在招销售，不找就最好的销售，你找以销售闻名的公司、然后去那找人、试图挖他们的 lieutenant 型，不一定他们的销售头。你觉得那好棋？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yes and no.
turns.zh: 既是也不是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ooh.
turns.zh: 哦。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yes and no, because I think if the organization is incredibly good at sales then the majority of the folks are probably amazing, but you always have weak links, and just because someone has a brand on their resume at the right time, I think oftentimes CEOs and founders will do this thing where they kind over generalize, well, Amazon's Prime team at this time was amazing or something like that. It's like, they definitely could have been, but just as any other company, there's going to be people that are breakout, top 1% type individuals, and then other individuals that get to ride the wave and reap the benefits of being at the right place at the right time. And I think that's a good starting place, but then also spending time getting a little bit deeper on who the best people are within that organization. But yeah, we always start with market mapping, so determining who the best companies are within a specific area, and then I just encourage everyone to take that a layer deeper.
turns.zh: 既是也不是，因为我觉得如果组织超会销售，那大多数人也许超棒，但你总有弱环，而只因某人简历上对的时候有个品牌，我觉得往往 CEO 和创始人会过度概括，嗯，Amazon 的 Prime 团队那时超棒或之类。像，他们绝对可能，但就像任何其他公司，会有 breakout、top 1% 型的人，然后其他搭浪、在对的时间对的地方 reap 好处的人。我觉得那是好起点，但也花时间更深一层搞清那组织里最好的人是谁。但对，我们总从市场地图（market mapping）开始，所以决定特定领域最好的公司是谁，然后我鼓励所有人再深一层。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. It just comes back to your previous piece of advice. Don't assume someone that has an awesome logo is going to be great, but sometimes they are. There's a question I should have asked you at the beginning that I'm going to ask now. How many folks have you placed? How many companies have you worked with? And then also, is there a story of just your favorite person that you've placed/company you've helped hire that comes to mind?
turns.zh: 懂了。它回到你之前的建议。别假设有超棒 logo 的人会超棒，但有时他们是。有个我该一开始问、现在问的问题。你安置了多少人？你和多少公司合作过？然后，有没有你安置的/帮雇的最爱的人或公司的故事想到？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah. So both great questions. I've placed probably 85 executives over the course of my career, and then lots of entry level employees when I was in house, and also some great key leaders. Yeah, probably 85 searches that I've opened and closed, so that's been incredibly fulfilling work. It's also fun too on the exec side of things because you hire the VP of engineering at Postmates and you see firsthand the product change. You know, you watch those types of things happen before your eyes, which is, it's fulfilling stuff, it's really cool.
turns.zh: 对。所以都好问题。我职业生涯安置了大概 85 个高管，然后我在内部时很多入门级员工，也有一些超棒关键领导者。对，大概 85 个我开和关的 search，所以那是极满足的工作。高管侧也趣，因为你雇 Postmates 的工程 VP、你 firsthand 看产品变。你知道，你亲眼看着那种事发生，那是满足的事，真酷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And delivery gets there faster too.
turns.zh: 配送也更快到那。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, exactly. So, that's really fun. Favorite placement of all time has got to be the VP of engineering that I placed at IRL, which is, to be completely honest, a big reason that I joined that company. Alex Strand is his name, and he is just the most incredible, atypical, high emotional intelligent engineering leader. Still super technical, but has managed teams in the hundreds, built out Amazon Prime Day, then went on to build the core messaging platform at Snapchat, called him and he was like, "Why would I ever leave? There's a ton of financial incentive and a team that I've built that all loves me."
turns.zh: 对，对，正是。所以，那真有趣。有史最爱的安置必须是我在 IRL 安置的工程 VP，老实说，是我加入那公司的大原因。他叫 Alex Strand，他只是最不可思议、非典型、高情商工程领导者。仍超技术，但管过几百人的团队、建过 Amazon Prime Day，然后去建 Snapchat 核心消息平台，call 他他说"我为什么要走？有大把财务激励、还有我建的、都爱我的团队。"

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: And we got him to ultimately make a move in two weeks, which is just kind of unheard of, although it ended up being like a seven month push for a start date, but that was a big reason why I went and joined IRL was to work side by side him and help build out his team and learn to get more deep on the technical side of things. Because oftentimes, on the executive level, as mentioned before, can be sometimes more of that people management type role. And so he just felt like this unique hybrid of an individual, and yeah, you close searches and you cross your fingers and hope for the best and feel very good about it, but he was one where I had all the confidence in the world that I could not have done better. You know? I just felt so great about that. So, that was a good one.
turns.zh: 我们最终让他两周内动，那有点前所未闻，虽然最终像七个月才到岗，但那是我去加入 IRL 的大原因——并肩和他、帮建他的团队、学技术侧更深。因为往往，如之前提的，高管级有时更多是那人员管理型角色。所以他感觉像这种独特的混合人，对，你关 search、交联手指、祝最好、感觉很好，但他是我对世界有信心我不可能做得更好的一个。知道吗？我就对他感觉超好。所以，那是好一个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know how much more confidence you could instill in a candidate joining a company than the recruiter also then joining the company.
turns.zh: 我不知道你能给加入公司的候选人多少更多信心，比招聘官也然后加入公司。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah, I did say that to him. I kept saying, "And if I were to go in house, I swear this is probably the company I would do it for." And then about four weeks after he signed, I'd texted him and I said, "Well, you'll never guess."
turns.zh: 对，我确实对他说过。我不断说"而如果我进内部，我发誓这大概就是我会为它做的公司。"然后他签了约四周后，我短信他说"嗯，你永远猜不到。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. What a stamp of confidence.
turns.zh: 惊人。多大的信心印记。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah. And a full circle life moment. I sent him a box of cookies, he sent it back and said, "Your turn."
turns.zh: 对。和 full circle 人生时刻。我寄他一盒饼干，他寄回说"轮到你了。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is he still there at IRL? Awesome.
turns.zh: 他还还在 IRL 吗？超棒。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yes, he is. He's great.
turns.zh: 对，在。他超棒。
