turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to shift a little bit to kind of flip to the product person's perspective and talk about, how do you be successful as a product leader in finding new opportunities and giving yourself opportunities in the space? And so maybe a first question is just generally, what should product leaders and PMs focus on to give themselves the most opportunity in their career?
turns.zh: 我想稍微转到产品人的视角、聊怎么作为产品领导者成功找新机会、给自己空间里的机会？所以也许第一个问题就一般，产品领导者和 PM 该聚焦什么给自己职业生涯最多机会？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: I think breadth is incredibly important. It's so critical, especially if someone has an end goal of wanting to step into a product leadership role to have been able to have touched lots of different components, as opposed to specializing in one specific thing. So I would say that's very important, to be able to make sure that you're maximizing opportunities for yourself down the road.
turns.zh: 我觉得广度（breadth）极重要。它关键，尤其如果有人终极目标是想 step into 产品领导角色、能触碰很多不同组件、而非专一具体事。所以我会说那非常重要，确保你最大化自己路上的机会。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: And then as mentioned before, just always keeping a pulse on the market, regardless of how happy you are in your current company, regardless of what the project is that you're so incredibly excited about that isn't going to conclude until Q1 of next year. It's just so important that you always know the companies that are doing great things and keep those windows open for people, because you never know what the next 12 months hold, and you want to be in a position where you're never running out the door looking for what's next, but rather being able to be super selective about the things that you have in front of you. And that comes with time and network building and relationship building over years, honestly.
turns.zh: 然后如之前提的，就一直保持市场脉搏，无论你在当前公司多开心，无论你超兴奋、要到明年 Q1 才结束的项目是什么。知道哪些公司在做大事、为人们开那些窗，太重要了，因为你永远不知道下 12 个月有什么，而你想处于你从不冲出门找下一步、而是能对你面前的东西超挑剔的位置。那随时间和网络建设、关系建设而来，老实说，经年。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And when you say breadth, are you saying things like work on the platform team for a bit, work on the user facing team, maybe the internal tools team, like different types of product, or something else?
turns.zh: 当你说广度，你是说像在平台团队干一阵、在面向用户的团队、也许内部工具团队、不同类型产品，还是别的？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Exactly that. Yeah. I think there's people that probably want to just be a specialist in growth, or want to get super deep on ads, and if that's the case, then by all means, do so. And I think there's something to be said about that as well because those types of skillsets will be needed. But if you're looking to diversify your skillset, continue to grow from a career trajectory perspective and think about potentially being in a head of product type role, I think it's really important that you touch all aspects of that.
turns.zh: 正是那个。对。我觉得有人大概就想当增长专家、或想超深搞广告，如果那样，那务必，去做。我觉得那也有可说之处，因为那些技能集会被需要。但如果你想多元化你的技能集、从职业轨迹角度继续成长、并想可能当产品负责人型角色，我觉得触碰那所有方面真重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm really happy to hear that because that's exactly the advice I give new PMs is that a variety of experience is one of the most powerful things you can do because you also just become a better PM because you can see how different types of products are built and how different types of teams operate and it just makes you better.
turns.zh: 我真高兴听那个，因为那正是我给新 PM 的建议——多样经验是你最有力的事之一，因为你也变成更好的 PM，因为你能看不同类型产品怎么建、不同类型团队怎么运作，就让你更好。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yes. Variety of experience, I think taking a bet on doing something more entrepreneurial, starting something, and then also joining things that are a little bit later and more established to get best practices. I think diversifying your skillset within an organization but also diversifying the work in which you're doing and the companies that you're spending time with is awesome.
turns.zh: 对。经验多样，我觉得对做更创业的事下注、起点事，然后也加入稍晚、更 established 的东西拿最佳实践。我觉得在组织内多元化你的技能集、但也多元化你做的工作和你花时间的公司，超棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So on that, something I'm always weary of is folks jumping around between all the fancy companies to get a bunch of logos on the resume. "Oh, I worked at Snap and Facebook and Netflix," and I feel like you're just building a resume and then your life flies by, and you forget that you should enjoy the things you're doing and work on things that are fulfilling and optimized for not a great resume. And, curious your thoughts on just how often you think you should move from company to company, one to optimize for opportunities in the future, or just generally, do you recommend people try to move around or go deeper at their company? There's a bunch of questions there, but take it wherever you want to.
turns.zh: 对。所以沿那个，我总 wary 的是人在所有 fancy 公司间跳、拿一堆 logo 在简历。"哦，我在 Snap、Facebook、Netflix 干过，"我觉得你就在建简历、然后你生命飞过、你忘了你该享受你做的事、做有满足感、不为好简历优化的事。而，好奇你的想法——你觉得你该多常换公司，一来为未来机会优化，或一般，你建议人试着四处动还是在本公司更深？那有一堆问题，但你想哪说哪。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. Okay. Sounds good. I think it's an interesting one because logo collecting is never something that you want to be known for, and the first thing you're taught, like entry level recruiting 101 is recognize patterns of candidates that jump from place to place and don't give opportunities a full chance. So, you're spot on. That is definitely not something you want to be known for if you're a prospect.
turns.zh: 对，对。好。听起来好。我觉得它有趣因为 logo 收集绝不是你想以之出名的事，而你学的第一件事——像入门招聘 101——是识别从一地到另一地跳、不给机会完整机会的候选人模式。所以，你 spot on。那绝对不是你想以之出名的事，如果你是 prospect。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: There's also something to be said about staying somewhere too long though. And I will say that. I think sometimes you find people that are almost loyal to a fault, and companies have tanked and all executives have left and the writing's on the wall, and they're holding onto the fact that they were hired by a really good guy or gal and they want to make it work because they care about the human being, and I think sometimes in your career you do have to be a little bit more selfish and think about what's going to be best for you in the long haul. And so maybe that is still keeping your head down and working hard while also being thoughtful about other things that are out there and not saying hard nos to opportunities that knock on your door.
turns.zh: 但也有事可说关于在某地待太久。我会说那。我觉得有时你发现人 almost 忠诚到 fault，公司垮了、所有高管走了、writing's on the wall，他们还抓着他们被超棒的人雇了、想让它 work 因为他们 care 那人，而我觉得有时你职业生涯你得有点更自私、想长期什么对你最好。所以也许仍是低头努力、同时也对其他在外的东西 thoughtful、不对敲你门的机会说硬 no。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So it's one where I would say it's an art and a science because you have to be thoughtful about taking on new things and knowing when it's worth taking a bet on yourself, but also you can't run as soon as things get hard because that is recognized, and if there's a riff or an internal dispute or a new leader brought in, and that is so quick as to make you run for the fences, that's not something that people look for because startup world is hard, tech is hard. Look at the crypto world right now. Things are incredibly volatile and difficult, and you want to be able to bring people in that are going to hang with you through the highs and lows.
turns.zh: 所以它是个艺术和科学的，因为你得 thoughtful 关于接新事、知道何时值得对自己下注，但也你不能在事一难就跑，因为那被认出，而如果有 riff 或内部争议或新领导者带来、那快得让你跑向 fence，那不是人找的，因为创业世界难、科技难。看 crypto 世界现在。事极波动难，而你想能带人进来陪你度过高低。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: We're always looking to see where people moved the needle, especially on the product side, where their fingerprints were, what they can actually point to that they did and are proud of during their time there. And so if all that they can say that they did was onboarded and moved on, then doesn't matter where you were, but it's not going to be something that I can at least stand on to cheer you on.
turns.zh: 我们总在看人哪里移动了指针，尤其产品侧，他们的指纹在哪、他们能实际指出的、他们做的、在那期间骄傲的。所以如果所有他们能说的他们做的是 onboarded 然后 moved on，那不管你在哪，都不会是我至少能站上为你欢呼的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like that. A lot of this comes down to, what impact have you made? And I was going to touch on that, and your point is, one, kind of heuristic for how long to stay at a place at the minimum is have some meaningful impact you can point to that you led. Does that sound right?
turns.zh: 我真喜欢那个。这很多落到，你造成了什么影响？而我打算触及那个，你的点是，一，关于最少待多久的启发式是有些你能指出的、你领导的Meaningful 影响。那听起来对？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And have that meaningful impact be something that others can speak to. I think that's huge. If you built something within the organization that you're proud of but no one knows about it, then that's more difficult to have as your stamp of approval for what you are able to accomplish there. But if you did something that cross-functional leaders were speaking to, that your team all sings the praises of, then that is something that you can put a feather in the cap and say, "Okay, I left this place better than I found it, and that's the reason that I have decided to move forward."
turns.zh: 对，正是。并让那 meaningful 影响是别人能说的。我觉得那巨大。如果你在组织内建了骄傲的东西但没人知道，那更难作为你能在那成就的批准印章。但如果你做了跨职能领导者说的、你团队都唱赞的事，那你能放羽毛在帽上、说"好，我留这地方比我发现它好，那是我决定前进的原因。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I imagine part of that is reference checks. People are going to check to see if you actually were successful.
turns.zh: 我想象那部分是背景调查（reference checks）。人会查你是否真成功。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: All the time. Yup. Whether you are exploratory, opportunistic, not looking at all, people are constantly calling each other, and the world of tech is so, so, so small, and no matter how fired up you were leaving a company or what went sideways, it is so critical that you try to leave the place better than you found it and do so as seamlessly as possible, because you want people to have nothing but positive to say. And oftentimes, that ... The thing that I always find too is if I call 10 people that were a part of the same organization as someone during a given period of time and they can't speak to anything they did, in that case, no news is not necessarily good news. You want to have an impact, you want to be able to say, "I did X, Y and Z. I'm super proud of this and the reason I moved on is because I did what I came in to accomplish."
turns.zh: 一直。对。无论你探索的、机会主义的、根本不在看，人一直互相 call，而科技世界这么、这么、这么小，无论你离开公司多火或什么走歪，你试图留那地方比发现它好、并尽可能无缝做，极关键，因为你想人只有正面可说。而往往，那……我也总发现的，如果我 call 10 个某时段同组织的人、他们不能说任何他们做的，那情况，没消息不一定是好消息。你想有影响，你想能说"我做了 X、Y、Z。我超骄傲这个、我前进的原因是我在我进来要成就的做了。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a little bit innately tricky for product leaders. I imagine you run into this, that sometimes you have to upset people as a product leader to get stuff done that needs to get done and maybe they disagree and then later it's like, okay, I see what you did. Is that true? Do you deal with that or is it generally like, oh, yeah, they're the great people everyone knows, like a hundred percent of people will say they're awesome?
turns.zh: 对产品领导者有点天生棘手。我想象你撞到这个，有时你得当产品领导者去 upset 人以完成需要完成的事、也许他们不同意、然后后来像"好，我懂你做的了。"是真的吗？你处理那个吗，还是一般像"哦对，他们是大家都知道的超棒人、100% 的人会说他们超棒"？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: It's a really good question. I think there's a way to navigate conflict without rubbing people the wrong way so that they'll say negative things. There's a way to be an impactful product leader and disagree and make change, and maybe your engineering leader and design leader and marketing leader completely disagree with the direction in which you're going, but because you have all of the data to support it and because you have gone about things in a way that feels very fact first and less emotional, it's really difficult for them to then point to why they disliked this person.
turns.zh: 好问题。我觉得有办法导航冲突而不 rub 人 wrong way 让他们说负面。有办法当有影响的产品领导者、不同意、做改变，也许你的工程领导者、设计领导者、营销领导者完全不同意你走的方向，但因为你有所有数据支持、因为你做的事感觉非常事实优先、少情绪，他们很难指为什么他们 dislike 这人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. This is interesting. So say you make those 10 calls, in your experience, the leaders you want to hire, are you finding 10 out of 10 are generally like, "Yes, this person's amazing, you should hire them"?
turns.zh: 对。这有趣。所以假设你做那 10 个 call，在你的经验，你想雇的领导者，你发现 10/10 一般像"对，这人超棒，你该雇"？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: There's ones that are slam dunks and no one has any negative to say. That's incredibly rare. More often you find some people like to just have something negative to say, just to have something negative to say. I also take all of my back channels with a grain of salt. Maybe the person I'm calling to back channel this person with I also haven't back channeled, right?
turns.zh: 有 slam dunk、没人任何负面说。那极罕见。更多是你发现有人就爱说点负面、就为说点负面。我也把我所有 back channel 都带盐（grain of salt）。也许我 call 去 back channel 这人的人我也没 back channel，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So every single thing that you hear, you just take, make note of, and then move on and think more holistically about. But I think typically what I would say is the glaring nos are very obvious. People that are polarizing individuals or have done wrong within an organization or made bad calls across the board are, you can get that information typically pretty quick.
turns.zh: 所以每个你听到的，你只拿、记、然后前进、更整体想。但我觉得通常我会说 glare 的 no 很明显。polarizing 的人、或在组织内做错、或全面做坏决定的，你通常很快拿到那信息。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: It's the mixed ones where it's, "I think that person was decent," those are pretty tough, and you need to really find people that worked super closely with them because otherwise it's pretty difficult to say whether or not they were able to make an impact. Which again comes back to why right off the bat it's so nice to just have people that you can tap within every organization that's like an academy company or a great company and say, "Point me in the direction of the three best people." I don't want to have to go through the burden of having to try and back channel all of the maybe middle 50% or what have you.
turns.zh: 是混合的那些——"我觉得那人还行"——那些相当难，你需要真找和他们超紧密工作的人，否则相当难说他们是否能造成影响。那 again 回到为什么一开始就 nice 有你能 tap 的人、在每个组织像 academy 公司或好公司、说"指我去三个最好的人方向。"我不想有负担试 back channel 所有也许中间 50% 或之类。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, most people don't have that, which is a reason to hire, work with a recruiter. You come build in with all of that network.
turns.zh: 对，大多人没那个，那是雇、和招聘官工作的原因。你带着所有那网络建入。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Totally. Totally there. Yeah.
turns.zh: 完全。完全在那。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a couple things I want to touch on that I wasn't planning to touch on, but reference calls. You do a lot of them, I imagine. And I'm curious, do you have any tips for how to ask questions on a reference call where you actually get useful advice where it's not just, "Yes, I like them, they're great. Hire them"?
turns.zh: 有几件事我想触及、我没计划触及，但背景电话。你做很多，我想象。而我好奇，你对背景电话问问题有什么 tips、能拿到有用建议而非只是"对，我喜欢他们，他们超棒。雇他们"？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Especially on references, provided references, I've only had two candidates where provided references have come back negative, which that's tough. Outside of that, typically references are a standard. It is important to dig pretty deep and ask the hard questions.
turns.zh: 尤其提供的参考（provided references），我只有两个候选人提供的参考回负面，那难。之外，通常参考是标准。深挖、问硬问题重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the hard questions?
turns.zh: 什么是硬问题？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah, why would I not hire this person? What are their biggest weaknesses? And then if they give you the typical, "Oh, if they work too hard," it's like, no, tell me more. What are their actual weaknesses? What are things that we should be really cognizant of? Would you hire this person again? Would you report to this person? Would you endorse this person if you knew that your name was attached to it? Things like that I think get people thinking, and even if you just sense the slightest pause, that in itself will be enough to make you think twice. Right?
turns.zh: 对。为什么我不会雇这人？他们最大弱点是什么？然后如果他们给你典型"哦，如果他们工作太努力"，像，不，多告诉我。他们的实际弱点是什么？我们该真注意的事什么？你会再雇这人吗？你会向这人报告吗？如果你知道你名字附着其上，你会 endorse 这人吗？这类事我觉得让人想，即使你只 sense 最微的停顿，那本身足够让你三思。对吧？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So it's a lot of reading the room and probing harder than you think necessary, which is tough. But back channel references I think will always provide a greater source of truth than provided. It's similar to an Instagram Reel as opposed to the photos you're tagged in. That's the way I think of it. It's like this is what you want the world to see or think of you as, and then these are what your peers and your direct reports and the people around you actually say about the work that you did during this time.
turns.zh: 所以是很多读场（reading the room）、比你以为必要的更深探，那难。但 back channel 参考我觉得总是比提供的更真源。它类似 Instagram Reel vs 你被 tag 的照片。那是我想它的方式。像这是你想世界看或想你成的，然后这些是你同行、你直接下属、你周围人实际说的你期间做的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Coming back to a point you made about recruiter training 101, you learn how to find patterns and red flags in people's resume. What else is a red flag in your resume that you want to avoid/there's a rule of thumb of like, if you're at a place for less than a year, it's bad. Is that true? How do you feel about that? How do hiring managers generally feel about that?
turns.zh: 太棒了。回到你提的招聘官培训 101，你学怎么找人简历的模式和红旗。还有什么简历里的红旗你想避免／有经验法则像"如果你在一地少于一年，坏。"是真的吗？你感觉怎样？hiring manager 一般感觉怎样？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: It definitely depends, with regards to being at a place less than a year. If that's a recurring theme, of course that's a big red flag. Even if it's happened two or three times, three definitely. If it's happened twice, it's like, "Huh, that feels off." You got to let people tell their story though and their side of things, and again, it comes back to reaching out to different people and understanding if what they're saying is true was actually the truth. And so when you have a really good pulse on what's happening in tech and whether there was a riff and the reason that person was let go was actually because they weren't prioritizing a certain part of the product or whatever, like those things, it happens. That's life, especially right now, right? If we were to X every single person that has a short stint that joined a new company over the course of the past year, that wouldn't do anyone any good.
turns.zh: 绝对取决于，关于在一地少于一年。如果那是反复主题，当然大红旗。即使发生两三次，三次绝对。如果发生两次，像"哈，那感觉 off。"你得让人讲他们的故事和他们的侧面，again，它回到 outreach 不同人、理解他们说的真不真。所以当你对科技在发生什么有好脉搏、是否有 riff、那人被 let go 的原因其实因为他们没优先产品某部分或之类，像那些事，发生。那是生活，尤其现在，对吧？如果我们 X 每个过去一年加入新公司短期的人，那不会对任何人好。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Another thing I've found that's pretty interesting is that people will often, because they're so afraid of that narrative, they'll often not include on their resume companies that they didn't stay for a year. And in my personal opinion, that's actually almost more of a red flag because that did happen, and you don't want to just pretend like that wasn't a decision you made in your life, and usually is handled with grace. You can speak to the reason that you decided to make a bet, the reason that you went there, and the reason that you moved on, in a way that people can typically resonate with. But I've seen executives just put that they've simply been advising for two years or something like that, when in reality they had two companies that failed.
turns.zh: 另一我发现相当有趣的是人常，因为他们那么怕那叙事，他们常不在简历包括他们没待满一年的公司。而我个人意见，那其实几乎是更大红旗，因为那确实发生，你不想就假装那不是你人生做的决定，而通常优雅处理。你能说你决定下注的原因、你去那的原因、你前进的原因，以人通常能共鸣的方式。但我看过高管就写他们简单在顾问两年或之类，而现实他们有两个失败公司。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: And the fact of the matter is, I have some CFO candidates I'm talking to right now and their past three years have been short stints because they were brought in to take a company through an IPO and then that changed, or they were brought in to enter into a SPAC and then that became less of the buzz. Right?
turns.zh: 而事实是，我有几个 CFO 候选人我现在聊、他们过去三年是短期因为被带进带公司过 IPO 然后那变、或他们被带进进 SPAC 然后那变少 buzz。对吧？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So these things happen and roles change, and I think it's just allowing people to tell their story is the most important thing. So I would say red flag is, for me, just always be honest about when you started, when you left a company. If I see that someone still has present on their LinkedIn but they've been gone for two years and they kind of are acting like they're still there, that doesn't feel good. Just want people to give you the truth, the straight facts, so that you can support them and tell their story and represent them in a way that makes you feel like you have all the details.
turns.zh: 所以这些事发生、角色变，我觉得就让人讲他们的故事是最重要的事。所以我会说红旗是，对我，就永远诚实关于你何时开始、何时离开公司。如果我看到某人 LinkedIn 仍写 present 但他们走了两年、他们有点像还在那，那感觉不好。就想人给你真相、直事实，好你能支持他们、讲他们的故事、以你有所有细节的方式代表他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So basically, don't lie. That makes sense. That reminds me a little bit of people kind of upgrade their titles a little bit because maybe they don't have an official title or they just want to sound a little important. How do you feel about when people do that on their resumes?
turns.zh: 懂了。所以基本，别撒谎。说得通。那有点让我想起人有点升级他们头衔，因为也许他们没官方头衔或就想听重点。你对人在简历那样感觉怎样？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah, I don't love that. I also don't love on the resume when people, and some people do this and it's okay, but when people say silly, vague names like they'll say something along the lines of, "Whatever at Reddit," as their title or, "Master of blank at this," and it's like, okay, what were you actually doing?
turns.zh: 对，我不爱那个。我也不爱简历上人——有些人做这个、没事——当人说傻、模糊名字像"Reddit 的 Whatever"作为他们头衔或"这的 blank 大师"，像，好，你实际在做什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But I think they do that to avoid recruiters reaching out to them.
turns.zh: 但我觉得他们那样做是为避招聘官 outreach 他们。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Exactly. As their direct target, I'm pissed. So I feel directly attacked in that regard. So that's something that throws me off, but that could definitely be a personal thing. And I think overall, for the most part, people don't have any other things that really just throw me for a loop. And the fact of the matter is, resumes we look at less and less, especially at the executive level, and it's a lot more of allowing people to tell their story, meeting in person, talking with their different people that support them, and getting kind of more of the big picture around who they are.
turns.zh: 正是。作为他们直接目标，我 pissed。所以那方面我感觉被直接攻击。所以那让我 off，但那绝对可能是个人的事。而我觉得整体，大多情况，人没其他真让我 loop 的事。而事实是，简历我们看越来越少，尤其高管级，更多是让人讲他们的故事、当面见、和他们不同支持的人聊、拿更全貌关于他们是谁。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk about what recruiters often do wrong and what you've learned there. But before we get there, one last question: do you have any tips for a product manager in the interviewing process, how to be more successful interviewing?
turns.zh: 我想聊招聘官常做错什么、你在那学到什么。但到那前，最后一个问题：你对产品管理者在面试流程有什么 tips、怎么更成功面试？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: I've had this come up a few times when I've interviewed product folks that they'll speak down on their counterparts or say that the reason they weren't able to meet deadlines or push product in the right way was because of the engineering team or because of other components of the business and it wasn't them. And so I think that's never a good way to go about it. So it seems obvious, but you would be surprised how not obvious it is.
turns.zh: 我有几次面试产品人时发生——他们会 speak down 他们的对手、或说他们不能 meet 截止或推产品对的方式的原因是因为工程团队或业务其他组件、不是他们。所以我觉得那绝不是好方式。所以似乎明显，但你会惊讶多不明显。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So thinking about things more holistically, speaking honestly about your strengths and things that you want to continue to grow and improve upon, and then being able to tell your story, like practice telling your story. So often people don't do that, especially when they're not looking for jobs, and then it's not until their 10th interview that they know how to tell their story and what they did and what they impacted and why they were someone to be missed when they moved on. Those are things that you want to know how to speak to, and unless it's something you've been doing or practicing, it's less natural. That's some advice I think just off the top of the head.
turns.zh: 所以更整体想事，诚实说你的优势和你想继续成长改进的，然后能讲你的故事，像练讲你的故事。往往人不做那个，尤其当他们不在找工作，然后直到第 10 次面试他们才知道怎么讲他们的故事、他们做的、影响的、为什么他们走时被 miss。那些是你该知道怎么说的，除非是你一直做或练的，它更不自然。那是些我脱口的建议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That's really good advice. One thing that makes me think about, I know I want to get to this last section, but do you think the best product leaders have their kind of story figured out in the future and work backwards from that and have a sense of where they want to end up, or just kind of take it as it goes? Because I'm the latter. I had no plan, I just went to see ... follow the path that was presented. Do you think that is generally true for folks that end up being successful, or do you recommend people think about, "Here's where I want to be in five years, here's what I need to do to get there"? Do you have any guidance there?
turns.zh: 太棒了。那真好的建议。一件事让我想，我知道我要到这最后部分，但你觉得最好的产品领导者有他们未来故事想好、从那往后推、有他们想终到的感觉，还是就随它去？因为我是后者。我没计划，我就去看……follow 呈现的路径。你觉得那对最终成功的人一般真吗，还是你建议人想"这是五年我想在的、这是我要做的到那"？你有任何指导？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: I mean, for what it's worth, I'm definitely more with you. I don't know where I want to be in five years, so it's tough for me to say. But I do think that typically someone that has the end goal of being a CEO will put the pieces into place to try and get there, and so it's not a bad idea if you do have an end goal of wanting to run your own thing to inch towards that. So maybe you go from being a product specific leader to then operating in some type of GM of a business unit capacity and owning a P&L, and then although it's more of a product oriented role, you're still getting closer and closer to that end goal of COO or CEO.
turns.zh: 我是说，值什么，我绝对更和你一起。我不知道五年我想在哪，所以难说。但我确实觉得通常有人终极目标当 CEO 会放拼图就试到那，所以如果你有终极目标想跑自己的事，朝那挪不坏主意。所以也许你从产品特定领导者到然后某类业务单元 GM 容量、own 一个 P&L，然后虽更是产品导向角色，你仍越来越近那 COO 或 CEO 终极目标。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So if it's something like that, then I think that naturally makes sense. Do think people can be enticed by shiny objects, so excited because it's a step up from a title perspective and things like that, and I think that's just so not important in the grand scheme of things. You could be the VP of product or a CPO of what, you know? That's so vague. If someone just says, "I want to be a chief product officer, that's the end goal," I always say, "Of what?" You could be the chief product officer of your household. Is it of a multi-billion dollar consumer brand or ...
turns.zh: 所以如果那样的事，那我觉得自然说得通。确实人能被闪亮东西 entice，所以兴奋因为是头衔视角的一步升、之类，而我觉得那在大局里那么不重要。你可能是产品 VP 或什么 CPO，知道吗？那模糊。如果人就说"我想当首席产品官，那是终极目标，"我总说"什么的？"你可能是你家的首席产品官。是十亿级消费品牌还是……

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So I guess what I'm trying to say is work backwards from a goal for sure, but don't allow titles or valuation bubbles or other things to derail something that feels good. If you're in a role and you feel like you're making an impact and you're learning and you're growing and are excited about the work you're doing, do not allow a title of some other company to make you feel like what you're doing isn't worthwhile.
turns.zh: 所以我猜我想说的是绝对从目标往后推，但别让头衔或估值泡沫或其他事 derail 感觉好的事。如果你在角色、感觉你在造成影响、你在学、你在成长、对你做的工作兴奋，别让别的公司头衔让你感觉你做的没价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. So many people just chase some fancy new role, new title, new logo, and end up getting there like, "Man, this sucks."
turns.zh: 我爱那建议。这么多人就追 fancy 新角色、新头衔、新 logo，到那像"老兄，这 sucks。"

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Exactly. Yeah.
turns.zh: 正是。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me, I did a meditation retreat once and one of the teachings there was you don't want to be fixated with achieving a specific thing, but you want to push your cart in that direction, just like head that direction and have a general sense, but not, "I need to be that thing and that's what'll make me happy."
turns.zh: 那让我想起，我有次做冥想 retreat，那一个教导是别 fixation 在达成特定事，但推你的车朝那方向，就朝那方向、有一般感觉，但不是"我需要是那事、那会让我开心。"

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Exactly. I think that's exactly right.
turns.zh: 正是。我觉得那完全对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. Final topic is from the recruiter perspective, what do you find recruiters do wrong most often or miss when they're trying to attract great product talent to a company?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好。最后话题从招聘官视角，你发现招聘官最常做错什么、或错过什么当他们试图吸引超棒产品人才到公司？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah, so this is one I feel especially passionate about because I do think recruiters have a bit of a reputation, and I think that it's for some good reason. There's naturally people that forget that these are human beings that we're dealing with every single day that have lives, have families, have careers, or ambitions outside of their career.
turns.zh: 对，所以这我特别 passionate 的，因为我确实觉得招聘官有点名声，而我觉得有些好理由。自然有人忘这些是每天我们打交道的真人、有生活、有家庭、有职业、或有职业外野心。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So I think it's essential that you remember that this is another human being on the other end of things and that you should treat them with the same level of respect that you would expect to be treated.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得必要你记得那是另一头的人、你该以你期望被对待的同水平尊重对待他们。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: This has become even more apparent now that I have gone through some of my own recruiting cycles where I was looking for different jobs, and a transactional recruiting call just will rub you so the wrong way and will make you want to put things on your resume like I just alluded to that say things like, "Whatever at Reddit," or what have you because you just don't want to deal with it.
turns.zh: 现在我更 apparent，因为我经历了些自己的招聘周期、我在找不同工作，而交易化招聘电话就 rub 你 wrong way、让你想在你简历放我刚暗指的说"Reddit 的 Whatever"或之类因为你就不想处理它。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: And so I think you have to be a human, you have to start with a relationship, find common ground, build rapport, listen to people, like actually listen, and remember what they say. So if someone says, "I never want to do a crypto company," and I just am only shoving crypto companies down their throat, that's just insanely tone deaf. Or if they say, "I have this vest that I really want to be around for in May of next year," and I just keep hitting them up prior to that, that's just so not receptive to what they just said.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得你得是人、你得从关系开始、找共同点、建融洽、听人、像真听、记得他们说的。所以如果人说"我绝不想做 crypto 公司"、而我只在塞 crypto 公司下他们喉，那 just insanely tone deaf。或如果他们说"我有这 vest 我真的很想待到明年五月"、而我就在那之前一直 hit 他们，那 just 不对他们刚说的 receptive。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Things like that, make notes if easier, because we speak to so many people all day long so it's definitely not easy to do. But I'll have a note on my calendar that John Kim's vest just happened in March, and then I'll be like, "Oh, okay, might be a good time for me to catch up." I won't say, "Congrats on the recent vest." I'll say, "You want to grab a coffee, or do you want to catch up about this?" Or, "Hey, I saw that you were speaking at this conference, love what you spoke about with regards to this." You got to find ways to connect with people outside of just shoving them into a job.
turns.zh: 像那样的事，更容易就记笔记，因为我们整天和这么多人说所以绝对不易做。但我会日历上记"John Kim 的 vest 刚三月发生，"然后我会"哦好，也许是我 catch up 的好时间。"我不会说"恭喜最近 vest。"我会说"你想喝咖啡吗，或你想 catch up 这事吗？"或"嘿，我看到你在这会议演讲，爱你说关于这的。"你得找方式和人连接、超出就把他们塞进工作。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: And so I would say something that I've learned and become very good at is starting with a foundation of relationship building, gaining trust from people, because once you have that, then people will hear you out on jobs and people will listen to you and actually trust your advice from a career direction and perspective, but that takes time to build that, and it's definitely not going to be built by just chucking things at the wall and seeing what sticks with people and seeing where you can shove them temporarily. In fact, that will make them lose trust. And once you lose trust in a candidate, it's impossible to get it back.
turns.zh: 所以我会说一件我学到、变得超好的，是从关系建设基础开始、从人赚信任，因为一旦你有那个，然后人会听你工作、人会听你、真信你从职业方向和视角给的建议，但那花时间建，绝对不会由只把东西砸墙看什么 stick 和人、看你能暂塞他们哪建。事实上，那会让他们失信任。而一旦你在候选人失信任，不可能拿回。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how one of the recurring themes of our chat so far is just play the long game in every way, which takes more time.
turns.zh: 有趣我们聊到这的反复主题就是每方面打长期游戏，花更多时间。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kind of sucks that you have to put in all this time ahead of time before you really need to get something done, but what you keep coming back to is just that's how you end up being successful as a recruiter, as a product leader, as a hiring manager, as a founder.
turns.zh: 有点 sucks 你不得不在真需要做事前投入所有这时间，但你一直回来的是就那是你作为招聘官、产品领导者、hiring manager、创始人成功的方式。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: A million percent. Yeah. Yeah. And it's really easy when you've got a quota to hit and you've got people to provide for and a mortgage to just think about the numbers, but you have to play the long game because people aren't just a commodity. It's so much more.
turns.zh: 一百万%。对。对。而有配额要达、有人要养、有房贷时，容易只想数字，但你得打长期游戏因为人不是商品。那是多得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And one of the perks of working with a recruiter is they have done that already for you, and so I was going to ask, when does it make sense for a founder to engage with a recruiter like yourself and when should they not?
turns.zh: 而和招聘官工作的一个好处是他们已为你做了那个，所以我想问，创始人何时该接触像你这样的招聘官、何时不该？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Engaging with recruiters sooner rather than later in a proactive way is always a positive thing. It's just sometimes companies aren't at the stage where they can necessarily hire a full-time recruiter because of resources and how expensive it is to bring in an exec recruiter.
turns.zh: 以主动方式、尽早而非晚接触招聘官总是正面事。只是有时公司没到能雇全职招聘官的阶段，因为资源和雇高管招聘官多贵。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So having someone that you can bounce things off of in a more informal capacity, bringing in someone like a talent advisor that can help in a consultative way, those types of things, a million percent. Leaning into the venture firms that have backed you, which is a lot of what I'm doing right now, that is definitely areas in which early CEO founders should be leaning into that and trying to get as knowledgeable as possible. And then I would say typically series B feels ... series A, dependent on the check size, and then series B feels like a good time to bring in a couple key big players, if the company's well positioned to do so.
turns.zh: 所以有你能非正式容量 bounce 事的人、带进像人才顾问能以咨询方式帮的人，那些事，一百万%。lean into 支持你的风投公司，那很多是我现在做的，那绝对早期 CEO 创始人该 lean into、试图尽量有知识。然后我会说通常 B 轮感觉……A 轮，取决于支票大小，然后 B 轮感觉是带几个关键大玩家（big players）的好时机，如果公司位置好能这样做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And bring in meaning full-time in-house recruiters or a firm?
turns.zh: 而带进意思是全职内部招聘官还是公司（firm）？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Probably bring in a firm. Yeah. That would be my recommendation. I think you can bring in one or two recruiters in the early days like seed, if it makes sense for the company and they're growing quickly, but it's all kind of case to case.
turns.zh: 大概带公司（firm）。对。那会是我的建议。我觉得早期像种子轮你能带一两个招聘官，如果对公司有意义、他们增长快，但都因案而异。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The fact that you're kind of off the table for most founders now that you're at GC, which is a part ... And is that true? Like you basically at this point work for General Catalyst founders, is that correct?
turns.zh: 事实是你现在对大多创始人 off the table 因为你在 GC，那是部分……那是真的吗？像你这时点基本为 General Catalyst 创始人工作，对吗？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: I am supporting all of our GC founders in the consumer and crypto portfolio. That being said, I spend all day every single day networking and chatting with amazing entrepreneurs, people that could be founding a company down the road and need some advice, great people that want to help in an advising capacity. So it is, I would say, 50% networking, 50% actual parachuting into portfolio.
turns.zh: 我支持我们所有 GC 在消费和 crypto 组合（portfolio）的创始人。话虽如此，我每天整天 networking、和超棒创业者聊、可能路上创公司需要建议的人、想顾问容量帮的伟人。所以它是，我会说，50% networking、50% 实际 parachuting 进组合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay.
turns.zh: 懂了。好。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Supporting them.
turns.zh: 支持他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's cool. I didn't know that part.
turns.zh: 那酷。我不知道那部分。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So outside of that, what do you suggest founders look for when they're looking for a recruiter, and the second to last question, what are signs that this is a good firm, a good recruiter? Just what should you be looking for when you're looking to hire a recruiter, either in house or a firm?
turns.zh: 所以之外，你建议创始人找招聘官时看什么，和倒数第二问题，什么信号这是好公司、好招聘官？就你找招聘官、内部或公司时该看什么？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: I think it's important to provide them with some direction and then see if they can recite it back to you. Tell them the types of things you're looking for and then say, "Did that resonate? Because I'd love to hear from you what you took away from that and what you think we should be looking for."
turns.zh: 我觉得给他们些方向、然后看他们能否 recite 回你重要。告诉他们你找的类型的事、然后说"那 resonate 吗？因为我爱听你从那带走什么、你觉得我们该找什么。"

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: And then kind of off the bat, ask them for a couple candidate ideas. Don't give them time to just go call other people. In real time, ask them for some candidate ideas. Where does their brain go? Who are people they would call tomorrow on this? The more that you can get that dynamic relationship formed before you even go to search, the more you can determine whether this is someone you want to calibrate with.
turns.zh: 然后有点一开始，问他们几个候选人想法。别给他们时间只去 call 别人。实时，问他们些候选人想法。他们脑子去哪？他们明天会 call 谁？你越能在去 search 前形成那动态关系，你越能决定这是你想校准的人。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So yeah, I think just putting them on the spot a little bit and asking them to show their work rather than just sending over a deck of searches that could have been done by other partners or could have just been done by other people on their team. You want to actually understand who this person is. So that first question is testing their listening skills and their ability to actually hear what you're saying and what you're looking for, and then the second is, okay, now how quickly can we get calibrated on what this profile should look like.
turns.zh: 所以对，我觉得就稍把他们放 spot、要他们 show 他们的工作、而非只发过可能其他合伙人或他们团队其他人做的 search deck。你想实际理解这人是谁。所以第一个问题测他们倾听技巧和他们真听你所说、你所找的能力，然后第二个是，好，现在多快我们能对这画像该长什么样校准。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That is great advice. Very tactical. Any final words or wisdom before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 太棒了。那好建议。非常落地。在我们到超刺激闪电轮前有任何最后的话或智慧？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: This has been awesome, by the way. I think more generally, the advice is just treat people like human beings, build rapport, play the long game, and gain trust, and that takes time. And so those are the most important things from a recruiting standpoint, is being able to tap people and have them feel like you genuinely have their best interest at heart and that you care about their career and life outside their career. And so I think that's what makes for a really good recruiter.
turns.zh: 这一直超棒，顺便。我觉得更一般，建议就是待人如人、建融洽、打长期游戏、赚信任，那花时间。所以那些是招聘视角最重要的，是能 tap 人、让他们感觉你真把他们最大利益放心上、你 care 他们职业和外职业的生活。所以我觉得那是成就好招聘官的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Simple advice, but often forgotten and easy to overlook. Awesome. All right. We've reached our very exciting lightning round. I'm going to give you six questions, whatever comes to mind, we'll go through them real fast. Does that sound good?
turns.zh: 简单建议，但常被忘、易忽视。太棒了。好。我们到超刺激闪电轮。我给你六个问题，想到什么说什么，我们快速过。听起来好？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Okay. Yes. Let's do it.
turns.zh: 好。对。来做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. What are two or three books that you recommend most to other people?
turns.zh: 来做。你最常推荐给别人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: The Power of Now and You Are Here.
turns.zh: 《当下的力量》（The Power of Now）和《你在这里》（You Are Here）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Awesome. What are favorite other podcasts that you listen to other than this one?
turns.zh: 哇。太棒了。除了这档，你听的其他最爱播客是什么？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: I mean, there's tech ones, but Your Own Backyard because I went to Cal Poly, so that one hits a little close to home.
turns.zh: 我是说，有科技的，但《Your Own Backyard》因为我上 Cal Poly，所以那有点 close to home。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I haven't heard of that. Cool. What's a recent movie or TV show that you've watched that you've enjoyed?
turns.zh: 哇，我没听过。酷。最近看、享受的电影或剧集是什么？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Top Gun I've watched too many times and-
turns.zh: 《壮志凌云》（Top Gun）我看了太多遍、和——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The new Top Gun.
turns.zh: 新《壮志凌云》（Top Gun）。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yeah. And then TV show. Oh, it's all trash reality, so I just can't tell you.
turns.zh: 对。然后剧集。哦，全是垃圾真人秀，所以我不能告诉你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I get that. I understand. My wife has that and she can't tell anyone. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我懂。我理解。我妻子有那个、她不能告诉任何人。对。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: That's my one secret.
turns.zh: 那是我一个秘密。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. Okay, great. We'll move on, but that's great. What's a favorite ... Oh, this is interesting. What's a favorite interview question that you like to ask or maybe you've seen someone ask?
turns.zh: 好。好，我们继续，但那很棒。什么最爱……哦，这有趣。你爱问或也许见过人问的最爱面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: I love the good strengths and weaknesses question. I think it's really good to see how people self-analyze themselves.
turns.zh: 我爱那好的优势和弱点问题。我觉得看人怎么自我分析超好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you look for in their answer that's the sign that it's well answered?
turns.zh: 你在他们答案里找什么、是答得好的信号？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Honesty, authenticity. Can read right through a, "Work too hard," answer or a perfectionist type answer. What are your weaknesses? Let's talk about it.
turns.zh: 诚实、真实。能直接看穿"工作太努力"或完美主义型答案。你的弱点是什么？我们聊聊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For real.
turns.zh: 说真的。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: So that one I think is always a really good test of character.
turns.zh: 所以那一个我觉得总是对品格的好测。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some favorite apps right now?
turns.zh: 现在最爱 App 是什么？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: I've been playing around on BeReal. I mean, I love Spotify, it's straightforward. And then I've been on Strava, I've been running, so that are the-
turns.zh: 我一直在玩 BeReal。我是说，我爱 Spotify，它直白。然后我在 Strava，我在跑步，所以那是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a good combination of apps. That's like a full life.
turns.zh: 那是 App 的好组合。那是完整生活。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Thank you. Thanks so much. Trying to be.
turns.zh: 谢谢。太感谢。试着是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. Who else in the industry would you say that you most respect as a leader and a thought leader influence type person?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。行业内你会说你最尊重的、作为领导者和思想领袖影响型的人是谁？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: My first boss out of college, Joe Suliman, is awesome. He's always taught me to lead with that relationship-based approach and it's really so easy to say that you do that, but then to actually do it and live it out for the people that work for you, as well as the people that are in industry and speak of you, is something else. And so he's always taught me to do that, and I just learned a ton from him and he's just incredibly smart and in tune with what's happening in industry and makes great stances and opinions on how to navigate those types of things. So, he's someone that I have an immense amount of respect for.
turns.zh: 我大学第一个老板 Joe Suliman，超棒。他总教我以那关系为基础的方式领导，而说你做那个真容易，但真做它、为你工作的人活出来，以及行业里的人、谈论你的人，是另一回事。所以他总教我做那个，我从他学了一吨、他超聪明、对行业发生什么 in tune、对怎么导航那些事做很棒的 stance 和意见。所以，他是我有巨大尊重的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds like an amazing person. Lauren, this was excellent. I feel like this is going to be useful to so many people, product managers, founders, other recruiters, all kinds of other people. Thank you so much for doing this and making the time. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out or maybe collaborate with you and learn more? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 听起来超棒的人。Lauren，这超好。我觉得这会对很多人有用——产品管理者、创始人、其他招聘官、各种其他人。非常感谢做这个、抽时间。两个最后问题。人们想联系或也许和你合作、学更多，能在哪线上找到你？听众怎么对你有用？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yes, absolutely. And also, thank you. This has been so much fun. They can reach out to me on LinkedIn. I happen to be on that one quite a bit, so definitely can DM me there, can send me an email, and I can shoot you that over as well. And then the way they can be helpful is if there's people that they think the world of, shoot them my way. If they have questions around best ways to go through an interview process or how to navigate different things, please, by all means, a huge part of my job is trying to help people that are going through this for the first time. Happy to just be a sounding board or of help in any capacity.
turns.zh: 对，绝对。也，谢谢。这一直这么有趣。他们能在 LinkedIn 联系我。我碰巧常在那，所以绝对能在那 DM 我、能发我邮件、我也能发你那个。然后他们能帮忙的方式是，如果有他们 world of 的人，发我来。如果他们对怎么过面试流程或怎么导航不同事有疑问，请，务必，我工作很大部分是帮第一次过这的人。高兴就当 sounding board 或任何容量帮。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So if you're an awesome product leader, you want to see what's out there, find Lauren on LinkedIn. Is that the best place to find you?
turns.zh: 所以如果你超棒产品领导者，你想看外面有什么，LinkedIn 找 Lauren。那是找你最好地方？

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: That's perfect.
turns.zh: 那完美。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. Awesome.
turns.zh: 好。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thanks, Lauren.
turns.zh: 谢谢，Lauren。

turns.speaker: Lauren Ipsen
turns.en: Thanks so much. Appreciate it.
turns.zh: 太感谢。感激。
